dependency_scope_checks: Theorem 2 uses Assumptions 1-5, the auxiliary-data construction (14)-(15), bar-tau, Omega and D, sparsity, oracle correction and its three local variance/moment quantities. No Assumption 6 or 7 is imposed.

Theorem 3 imports the setup of Theorem 2 and its bias conclusion (i). It uses population tau, sigma and rho, and sigma_mu. Do not import bar-sigma or bar-rho merely because Theorem 2's distinct Gaussian conclusion uses them. Record the subpart reference explicitly.

Theorem 4 uses Assumptions 1-7, the cross-fit construction and interval, fold events, concatenated corrections, oracle correction and b_n. Its all-alpha conditional coverage statement holds on one event; do not replace it by separate pointwise guarantees.

Theorem 5 imports the estimator construction and tuning from Theorem 4, then explicitly assumes only 1-5. Do not propagate Assumptions 6-7 or the confidence interval merely through the theorem citation. Its approximation error concerns initial tilde-mu, not the optimized mu-hat.

The multi-split estimator and numerical algorithms in Sections 4-6 are not the estimator construction asserted by Theorems 2-5. Do not add their proof or implementation details as statement dependencies.
source_issues_to_resolve_or_record: Zero variance denominators can occur without Assumption 7, including sigma_mu=0 under perfect correction. Preserve the original formulas and record any absent degeneracy convention; do not impose positivity silently.

Theorem 3 does not repeat m in its preamble but references Theorem 2(i), whose probability bound uses it. Retain the inherited scope explicitly.
Theorem 4 tuning uses printed n in sqrt(log(p)/n), whereas individual fold samples have n/3 observations. Preserve the printed full-sample notation and constant convention.
Assumption 7 bounds marginal residual variances; do not replace it by a uniform conditional variance lower bound.
Theorem 3 asserts E(zeta_1*zeta_2|D)=0, not independence. Its first normal approximation is conditional and its second is marginal; their sum is not automatically marginally Gaussian.
